newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan cuts China exchanges, but denies protest.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan cuts China exchanges, but denies protest.

text.p: Taiwan's cabinet has cancelled budgets for five exchanges with arch-rival China, but officials denied a newspaper report on Tuesday that Taipei was protesting against Beijing's tightening diplomatic embargo.
A senior transport ministry official acknowledged that funds for the planned programmes had been killed, but insisted the move had no political implications.
"The cabinet also cut the budgets for other plans -- not just those five," Hsieh Ming-hui, head of the ministry's navigation and aviation department, told Reuters by telephone.
The cut would result in the suspension of five transport ministry programmes to increase exchanges with China, a rival of Taiwan since a civil war split them in 1949.
Taipei's China Times Express daily said the government was irked by Beijing's drive to squeeze Taiwan out of international diplomatic circles and cut the budgets to voice its protest.
Hsieh played down the idea that the cuts were a reprisal.
"I don't think there are any political implications," he said without further elaboration.
Nationalist-ruled Taiwan has banned direct contacts with China's communist government since 1949, but has allowed a range of "unofficial" exchanges in the interest of better ties.
Numerous senior mainland officials were able to visit Taiwan in 1996 under such informal exchanges despite acute military tensions across the Taiwan strait.

The transport ministry programmes, set for fiscal 1997/98 (June-July), would have sent Taiwan aviation officials to China to negotiate with their mainland counterparts on future cross-strait aviation business, the newspaper said.

Other programmes suspended because of the cut included sending navigation officials to China to survey shipping and seaman administration systems, and sponsoring cross-strait seminars on shipping and shipwreck management, it said.
The China Times Express gave no total for the budgets that were eliminated, but said T$422,500 (US$15,360) in funds to send five officials to China had been vetoed.

China, which regards Taiwan as a renegade province that must be brought under Beijing's rule, maintains that Taiwan has no rights to participate in international affairs and pressures other countries not to forge ties with the Nationalist island.

In early January, China used its U.N. Security Council veto to block a proposal to send a peace-keeping mission to Guatemala, a move seen as pressuring Guatemala to review its diplomatic ties with Taiwan.
Taiwan has only 30 diplomatic allies, the biggest of which, South Africa, has announced plans to sever formal relations with Taipei in favour of Beijing in 1997.
